newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian economic emergency seen hurting industry.
newsitem.headline: Colombian economic emergency seen hurting industry.

text.p: An overwhelming majority of Colombian industrialists believe the economic emergency measures declared this month by President Ernesto Samper are bad news for business, according to a survey published Friday.

The survey, commissioned by the National Bankers' Association (ANIF) and published in Bogota's El Espectador newspaper, is based on responses from 129 industrialists across the country and was conducted from Jan. 20-24.
More than 95 percent of respondents said the measures would have a negative impact on their businesses while only 1.6 percent viewed them as positive.

Measures decreed as part of the emergency that Samper declared on Jan. 13 include a 6 percent tax on new foreign loans to help curb the huge inflow of dollars that caused the peso to appreciate by 16 percent in real terms last year.
The stronger peso hurt exporters by eroding the real value of export revenues and making their goods less attractive abroad.
But the tax on new loans has been widely criticized by importers, who finance much of their business with foreign credits.
The government has said the tax was necessary to halt last year's sudden influx of dollars, especially in December.

But central bank chief Roberto Junguito told reporters Thursday that 74 percent of the foreign capital that entered the country late last year stemmed from privatization revenues and government debt sales.
Colombia's Constitutional Court has 90 days, from the date the emergency measures were announced, to determine whether they were justified and should remain in effect.
